title: SLO portfolio hedging toolkit
author: Aisha Malik
body:
Summary
=======
This toolkit defines patterns and operational tooling for SRE teams to 'hedge' an SLO portfolio that spans heterogeneous inference workloads (text generation latency, embedding throughput, and batch reranking). Hedging means building conservative guards — telemetry, capacity buffers, and automated mitigations — so that a portfolio of SLOs remains stable under model variance, tenant bursts, and infrastructure churn.

Motivation
----------
Redwood runs many inference tenants with varying criticality. Individual SLOs (e.g., p95 latency, availability, embedding throughput) interact: a bursty tenant can spike queue length and cause tail latency regressions across unrelated model families. Traditional single-service SLO responses (raise paging when burn high) are insufficient. We require a set of pragmatic hedges that:
- Maintain customer-facing SLOs during transient shocks
- Protect high-priority tenants from noisy neighbors
- Give operators clear, automatable actions to reclaim budget or shed load

Scope and applicability
----------------------
This document applies to Redwood’s inference services hosted and dedicated modes (Redwood API and Dedicated GPU pools). It covers:
- SLO composition guidance across availability/latency/throughput
- Error budget hedging policies and burn-rate thresholds
- Capacity-side mitigations (burst pools, preemptible nodes, rate-limited fallback)
- Operational tooling: alerts, dashboards, and automated playbooks
- Runbook excerpts for hedging actions and verification steps

Definitions and conventions
---------------------------
- SLO: service-level objective (e.g., request latency p95 < 300ms for hosted-text-gen).
- Error budget: permissible SLO violation window (1 - SLO) over the rolling window (typically 30d / 7d)
- Hedging window: an early-intervention timeframe (1h–6h) where pre-emptive mitigations are allowed
- Burn-rate: rate at which the error budget is being consumed; expressed relative to baseline (1x)

Design patterns for SLO portfolios
----------------------------------
1) Prioritized SLO tiers
   - Tier 0 (Critical): customer-facing low-latency endpoints with SLA (99.95% availability, latency p95 < 250ms).
   - Tier 1 (Standard): interactive endpoints without enterprise SLA (99.9% availability, latency p95 < 400ms).
   - Tier 2 (Best-effort): internal batch/async workloads (no strict latency guarantee, throughput targets).
   Assign each SLO a tier and a tenant priority label. Hedging decisions prefer protecting higher tiers.

2) Portfolio-level invariants (examples)
   - Availability invariant: >= 99.9% of Tier 0 endpoints must be healthy across regions.
   - Tail invariant: median of per-tenant p95 tail ratio to baseline must be < 1.5x.
   - Throughput invariant: aggregate embedding pipeline throughput must remain >= 85% of baseline over 1h.

Error budget hedging strategies
------------------------------
A) Early-warning burn classification
   - Low burn: burn-rate < 3x (notify owners, run synthetic canary).
   - Medium burn: 3x <= burn-rate < 10x (auto-annotate incidents, run targeted cache warm, throttle low-priority tenants).
   - High burn: burn-rate >= 10x (execute aggressive hedges: tenant eviction to burst pool, model fallback to smaller variant, traffic shaping).

B) Hedging primitives (actions)
   - Priority-based rate limiting: apply token-bucket limits to Tier 2 tenants when cluster queue depth > 90th percentile threshold.
   - Model fallback: automatically route requests to quantized/compact variant with verified quality profile when latency SLOs breach.
   - Burst pool offload: move eligible requests to preprovisioned burst GPU pool (with cost accounting).
   - Cache seeding and KV-prefetch: warm KV cache for hot prompts via synthetic traffic at reduced priority.
   - Graceful degradation pages: serve brief maintenance placeholders for non-critical endpoints to prevent cascading failure.

Operational tooling specifications
--------------------------------
Telemetry and dashboards
  - SLO portfolio dashboard (per-region, per-tenant):
    * Columns: tenant, tier, SLO, rolling-window-error-budget%, burn-rate(1h/6h), p50/p95/p99 latency, queue depth, GPU utilization, kv-cache-hit%
    * Heatmap coloring: green < 20% consumed, amber 20–60%, red > 60%
  - PromQL examples (Grafana/Thanos):
    * error_budget_percent = 100 * (1 - (sum(errors[30d]) / sum(requests[30d])))
    * burn_rate_1h = increase(errors[1h]) / max(1, (error_budget_allowance / 30))
    * queue_depth_alert = avg_over_time(inference_queue_length[5m]) > 200

Alerts and runbook integration
  - Alert types and thresholds:
    1) SLO-Burn: burn_rate_1h > 3x for 30m -> P3 notify owners + create incident record.
    2) SLO-Portfolio: >25% of Tier 0 endpoints in region degrade beyond p95 SLA -> P2 paging and pre-mitigation.
    3) Queue-Pressure: average queue depth > 90th percentile for 15m -> P1 immediate auto-mitigation trigger.
  - Each alert includes a link to the hedging-runbook and a one-click mitigation button (see automation section).

Automation and safe-guards
  - Automation primitives must be idempotent and reversible. For each automated hedge record: owner, precondition PromQL, action (k8s API/traffic rule), and rollback action.
  - Example automation (pseudo YAML):
    # Auto-evict low-priority tenants into burst pool
    precondition: "avg_over_time(inference_queue_length[5m]) > 250 and burn_rate_1h > 10"
    action: "post /api/v1/tenants/{tenant}/evict -> {target_pool: burst-pool-1}"
    rollback: "restore traffic-groups after 30m or when burn_rate_1h < 1.5"

Hedging runbook (operator steps)
--------------------------------
Primary goal: restore portfolio invariants while preserving high-tier availability.
1) Triage (owner on page)
   - Confirm alert context and region, validate burn-rate using SLO dashboard.
   - Check related telemetry: model load, GPU OOM events, network retries, cache hit ratio.
2) Quick safe mitigations (first 10 minutes)
   - Execute automatic cache seeding for hot keyspaces.
   - Apply per-tenant soft rate limit (10–20% reduction) for Tier 2 tenants.
   - If queue depth still rising -> enable model fallback for a small subset (5–10%) of traffic for affected endpoints.
3) Aggressive mitigations (10–60 minutes)
   - Evict noisy tenants to the burst pool and enable explicit cost alerting for them.
   - If degradation persists, perform cross-region partial failover for Tier 0 endpoints.
4) Stabilization and learning (>60 minutes)
   - Keep mitigations in place until error budget burn_rate_1h < 1.5 for two consecutive 15m windows.
   - Record actions in incident system and tag SLO owners.

Verification checklist
----------------------
- SLO portfolio dashboard shows burn-rate dropping and queue depth trending down.
- Tier 0 p95 restored and stable for 30 minutes.
- No new GPU OOM or kernel crashes reported.
- Automated rollback schedule created (or manual rollback approved).

Post-incident actions and evidence
--------------------------------
- Attach the following evidence to post-incident review:
  * SLO burn timeline export (CSV) for 7d window
  * Prometheus traces and flamegraph for top-3 latency goroutines
  * k8s pod restart and eviction logs
  * Automated mitigation audit (who/what/when/rollback)
- Run a targeted regression test against model variants used in fallback to validate quality regressions below the customer-defined threshold.

Implementation checklist for platform engineers
----------------------------------------------
1) Dashboard: implement SLO portfolio view in Grafana with heatmap and per-tenant filters.
2) Alerts: add Prometheus rules and tie them to the incident automation service.
3) Automation: implement REST hooks for tenant evict/restore and model fallback; ensure auth via service account.
4) Synthetic canaries: add per-route canary probes that validate latency and model output sanity.
5) Cost accounting: tag all burst-pool ops for billing attribution.

Appendix A — Example SLOs and hedging thresholds
------------------------------------------------
| SLO name | Tier | Rolling window | SLO target | Hedging burn thresholds | Notes |
| Hosted-text-gen-latency | Tier 0 | 30d | p95 < 250ms | Low: 2x, Medium: 5x, High: 12x | fallback to q8_compat model allowed only for non-enterprise tenants |
| Embedding-throughput | Tier 1 | 7d | 95% of baseline over 1h | Low: 1.5x, Medium: 4x, High: 10x | prioritize high-recall tenants |

Appendix B — Sample PromQL snippets
-----------------------------------
# 1h burn rate (errors = status >= 500)
burn_rate_1h = increase(inference_errors_total[1h]) / max(1, (0.01 * sum(inference_requests_total[30d]) / 30))

# Queue pressure alert
avg_queue_5m = avg_over_time(inference_queue_length[5m])

Appendix C — Quick CLI mitigations
----------------------------------
# Soft rate limit a tenant (example)
redwoodctl tenant set-rate-limit --tenant-id tenant-42 --requests-per-second 20 --priority soft-limit --reason "SLO portfolio hedging"

# Evict tenant to burst pool
redwoodctl tenant evict --tenant-id tenant-42 --target-pool burst-pool-1 --duration 30m --annotate "auto-hedge"

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Primary owner: eng-sre (SLO portfolio squad).
- Secondary owners: serving-runtime and platform-autonomy teams.
- Review cadence: quarterly review of hedging thresholds and burst-pool sizing.
